Washington — A Republican-led effort to approve a House-passed stock trading bill fell short in the Senate on Wednesday, with Democrats arguing the restrictions don't go far enough while pushing back against a voter ID provision that they argue would gut mail voting.
In a 53 to 47 vote that fell along party lines, the measure failed to reach a 60-vote threshold needed to advance.
The bill, known as the Stop Insider Trading Act, passed the House in July with the support of all Republicans and 13 Democrats. It would prohibit lawmakers, their spouses and dependent children, from purchasing publicly traded stocks, while requiring that they publicly disclose each intended sale at least a week in advance to limit their ability to profit off insider information.
But Democrats argued that the bill doesn't go far enough, urging that an outright ban is needed for members of Congress — along with the president and members of his administration.
"The Republican toothless stock-trading bill is as ineffective as a screen door on a submarine," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said on the Senate floor ahead of the vote. "And let's be clear: they don't even want it to pass. They designed the bill to fail."
The New York Democrat railed against the legislation earlier this week, while noting it wouldn't apply to the executive branch. He claimed that Republicans "carved the White House out of their supposed crack down on corruption."
Democrats also saw the bill's provision requiring voters to show photo identification when voting in federal elections as a poison pill designed to prompt them to vote against the more popular stock-trading restrictions. The unrelated provision was included in the bill as President Trump has put pressure on Congress to approve elections-related legislation ahead of the midterms.
GOP leaders moved ahead with the vote on Wednesday as senators prepare to leave town to hit the campaign trail, bringing up the vote alongside another bill aimed at shielding Americans from energy costs attributed to data centers later in the day. The votes, which were expected to fall short, aimed to put Democrats on the record on the issues at a time when Senate Republicans face several races that have grown more competitive, putting control of the upper chamber next year into question.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, called the bill a "common-sense piece of legislation," pointing to its limits on stock trading and the voter ID requirement.
"It's a pretty simple measure," Thune said. "But an important way to ensure that members of Congress are held to the standards that America should be able to expect of their representatives."
Lawmakers have pursued a number of efforts to ban congressional stock trading in recent years. But Schumer argued that the latest bill "isn't a stock-trading ban, it's Republicans' last-ditch effort to save face." If Republicans want to ban stock trading, the New York Democrat said his caucus is "ready to go."

articles.title_orig: Senate Democrats block House-passed data center bill aimed at addressing energy costs
articles.title_zh: Senate Democrats block House-passed data center bill aimed at addressing energy costs
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked a GOP-led effort to advance a bill aimed at shielding Americans from energy costs attributed to data centers, despite the bill securing widespread bipartisan support in the House earlier this month.
In a 57 to 43 vote, all but four Democrats — Sens. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock of Georgia — opposed the measure, arguing that the bill would make the protections for Americans "optional."
"While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said. "We need real action on data centers, and what do Republicans decide all of a sudden to push forward? A bill that is totally optional."
The outcome denies Republicans a legislative victory just weeks before the midterm elections. Voters across the U.S. have become increasingly opposed to the construction of data centers, which provide the computing power needed to fuel the AI boom. But Republicans argued that the vote would put Democrats on the record on the issue that has gained traction in recent months.
The bill, titled the Ratepayer Protection Act , seeks to put the costs of new energy infrastructure used for data centers on companies, rather than passing costs on to consumers. But it would only require state utility regulators to consider standards to hold companies responsible for the costs, which Senate Democrats argue doesn't go far enough.
The measure passed the House earlier this month in a 417 to 3 vote.
Asked about House Democrats' support for the measure, and why Senate Democrats aren't on the same page, Schumer said "we don't vote for frauds."
Schumer stressed that the measure sets up a voluntary system, saying, "Not a single company has to comply with it." He argued that if Republicans wanted a real solution, including GOP Sen. Jon Husted, who has led the push in the Senate, they should take up legislation put forward by one of his Democratic colleagues "that is real and has teeth."
"They want it optional, which means zero," Schumer said. "We want it mandatory."
Husted is locked in a competitive Senate race in Ohio against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, and has faced scrutiny for his previous support for data centers. The Senate GOP campaign arm warned in a memo last month that more than anything else, the data center issue is the "anchor hanging around Husted's neck."
Earlier this month, Husted sought to approve the same bill under unanimous consent, which gives any single lawmaker the power to block its passage. But Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, the top Democrat on the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, proposed that the Senate instead pass his own bill that he said is "what is needed to start to bring down energy prices." Ohio's other senator objected to Heinrich's bill.
Wednesday's vote came as senators are preparing to leave town this week and hit the campaign trail. Senate Republicans teed up the vote alongside an effort to pass legislation to limit congressional stock trading, which Democrats also blocked.
Speaking on the floor ahead of the vote on the data center legislation, Heinrich said "this is nothing more than a messaging bill on the eve of an election."
"Congress needs to pass a law with real teeth," he added.

Russia’s warning that it could resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempts to isolate Kaliningrad is raising new concerns that the heavily militarized Russian exclave could become a flashpoint between Moscow and the alliance, as experts warn the territory is already being used to pressure Europe through hybrid warfare.
Moscow warned NATO in a diplomatic document that it was prepared to use "the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons" if alliance members attempted to isolate Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia, Reuters reported Wednesday.
Kaliningrad, a Russian territory geographically separated from the Russian mainland, sits on the Baltic Sea between NATO members Poland and Lithuania and hosts significant Russian military assets, including elements of Moscow’s Baltic Fleet.

The Russian document also raised the possibility of strikes against "decision-making centers" in NATO member states from the outset of a conflict.
NATO rejected Moscow’s allegations in a response reviewed by Fox News Digital, saying the alliance is defensive and that none of its exercises or activities threaten Russian territory. The alliance also urged Russia to stop its "irresponsible nuclear rhetoric."
Carrie Filipetti, executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, a nonpartisan network of foreign policy leaders, told Fox News Digital that Moscow has repeatedly used nuclear threats as a means of trying to deter Western support for Ukraine.
"Russia has threatened to use nuclear weapons in the past, including veiled references to tactical nuclear attacks at the beginning of Putin's invasion of Ukraine , lowering their formal threshold for launching a nuclear attack in 2024, placing Russia's nuclear forces on high alert, and restarting nuclear testing," Filipetti said. "It is very common for Putin to use these threats, because he sees it as a way to deter Europe and the United States from continuing to support Ukraine."

"The threat about a nuclear attack if Kaliningrad is threatened or isolated comes on the heels of a few developments," she added, pointing to NATO jets being scrambled over Russian aircraft, U.S. and NATO air drills near Kaliningrad last month, and heightened tensions over the war in Ukraine.
Filipetti, who also served as a deputy assistant secretary at the State Department and as a senior policy advisor for the United States Mission to the United Nations (USUN), argued that the timing also reflects mounting pressure on Moscow as the war continues.
"Putin seems to understand that the tide is turning against him, and he's resorting to aggressive rhetoric to try to stop European support for Ukraine as he has tried to do in the past," she said.
Dr. Azeem Ibrahim, a research professor at the Strategic Studies Institute at the U.S. Army War College and chief strategy officer at the New Lines Institute, told Fox News Digital that NATO should take the warning seriously, particularly because of the broader role Kaliningrad is already playing in Moscow’s confrontation with Europe.

"Russia is actually adopting a very different approach," he said, describing a strategy of hybrid warfare targeting "infrastructure" and "societies in general — what keeps societies functioning."
Ibrahim described Kaliningrad as the "front line" of that effort.
"It’s essentially become a Russian fortress," he said. "This is essentially a front-line operation of the Russians in terms of signals intelligence, signals interference and essentially mechanisms by which to carry out this hybrid warfare."
Such interference, Ibrahim said, could play a role in the broader confrontation by disrupting civilian communications and infrastructure before or alongside a conventional military attack.
"All of that would be preceded by interference operations like this to ensure that societies are not functioning, are not able to respond to emergency services, the news information services, etc.," Ibrahim said. "So governments lose control over what actually makes societies function."

The challenge for NATO, he said, is that such operations can be more difficult to attribute than a conventional assault.
"Many times, you cannot trace exactly where a lot of this interference is actually coming from — attacks on power stations or internet and telecommunications, et cetera," Ibrahim said. "There’s always some sort of plausible deniability if it’s done by an actor who's very capable."
The ambiguity, Ibrahim argued, presents a challenge for an alliance built around collective defense against armed attack.
"NATO really does have to kind of reconfigure its posture to understand that these kinds of attacks are equivalent to essentially any sort of kinetic attack," he said.
Asked what NATO and neighboring Poland and Lithuania should do following Russia’s warning, Ibrahim called for the alliance to establish clearer consequences for hybrid attacks.
"We now need to start going on the offensive in terms of hybrid warfare and understanding the threat and pushing back and sending a very clear signal to Moscow that such threats will not stand," he said, arguing that a sufficiently serious hybrid attack should be considered capable of triggering NATO’s Article 5 collective-defense clause.
Lithuania, which directly borders Kaliningrad, rejected Moscow’s warning and accused Russia of trying to undermine NATO unity and Western support for Ukraine.
"Russia’s insinuations and threats have no basis. NATO is a defensive alliance and poses no threat to Russia or any other country," Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry told Fox News Digital. The ministry added: "We strongly condemn any threats to use force and irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. Russia must stop its aggression against Ukraine… Lithuania is strengthening its national defense system and capabilities, including air defense," the ministry said. "We train with our allies and work alongside NATO forces deployed in Lithuania. We are prepared to defend every inch of NATO territory and respond to any threats."

articles.title_zh: Senate Democrats block Sen. Husted-led bill on data centers, calling it ‘toothless’
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Senate Democrats blocked legislation Wednesday aimed at protecting consumers from paying higher prices when new data centers are built in their communities.
The vote was 57-43, short of the 60 needed to break a filibuster.
The Ratepayer Protection Act , which passed the House by a vote of 417-3 two weeks ago, sets a federal standard on the issue. It also instructs state public utility commissions to find ways to make developers of data centers that use huge amounts of energy cover their own costs of water and electricity to consumers.
The Senate version is led by appointed Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who’s locked in a competitive battle as he seeks his first full Senate term. He’s facing heat at home from Democratic rival and former senator Sherrod Brown, who has branded him “the face of data centers” for promoting developments when he was lieutenant governor.
“I heard they said they wanted lower electricity prices,” Husted said of Democrats on Tuesday. “All they have to do is not block it, vote for it, and it will be on the president’s desk, and we will have a bipartisan win.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the bill is merely “optional” for states and won’t achieve much beyond partisan messaging for Republicans.
“Plain and simple, the Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday. “It does not require any protections at all. While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill. We need real action on data centers.”
Schumer said Republicans should instead take up bills by Sens. Chris Van Hollen , D-Md., and Martin Heinrich , D-N.M., that would go further in imposing cost-related rules on data centers.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., rejected Democratic arguments that the bill is simply a Republican political move to protect Husted’s re-election bid. He noted that nearly every House Democrat voted for the measure.
“I don’t know how you can say something that passed the House of Representatives 417-3 isn’t consequential,” Thune told reporters. “AOC voted for it over there. Hakeem Jeffries voted for it over there. This is a bill that could go to the president and become law. Evidently, a lot of Democrats in the House of Representatives thought it was important to be for and thought that it did exactly what the bill says it does.”
An NBC News poll this month found that data centers are unpopular: By nearly 6 to 1, voters said they’d be less likely to vote for a candidate who supports building a data center in their community. The survey found that voters trust Democrats over Republicans by a margin of 12 points to deal with data centers.
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring, said Husted was “right to get the message out” on data center costs.
But when asked if the bill would achieve much beyond that, Tillis said, “No.”
“I think the best way to deal with this is ... down in North Carolina, most utilities are managed through public utility commissions,” Tillis said. “They’re managed through local and state decision-making. That’s where it should be.”
Sahil Kapur is a senior national political reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Scrubs Season 2 TV Review: The sitcom revival gets better with bigger roles for legacy characters
articles.title_zh: Scrubs Season 2 TV Review: The sitcom revival gets better with bigger roles for legacy characters
articles.content_orig:
Plot : J.D. enlists Turk and Elliot to help with Dr. Cox’s care. Meanwhile, Elliot finds an unexpected burst of confidence years in the making.
Review : The first season of the Scrubs revival was a welcome return to Sacred Heart Hospital and our favorite characters, JD, Elliot, and Turk. With some new faces in the cast as well as returning old ones, it was a massive improvement over the lackluster final seasons of the original run of Scrubs and ranked easily amongst the best revivals ever. It was not a foregone conclusion that there would be a second season of the Scrubs revival, but thankfully, it’s back for a new run of 10 episodes, one episode longer than the initial season. Having seen the first episodes of the new season, it feels like a natural continuation of where we were last season, which concluded just five months ago.
This new season of Scrubs brings back most of the characters introduced in season one, including Jacob Dudman as Asher, David Gridley as Blake, Layla Mohammadi as Amara, and Amanda Morrow as Dashana. Ava Bunn, who played Dr. Tosh, has been upped to series regular while her fellow interns remain in a recurring capacity. While Judy Reyes is back as Carla, she appears in a far more limited capacity, while John C. McGinley is a central figure as Dr. Cox’s medical diagnosis introduced last season becomes an ongoing subplot in this sophomore run. McGinley looks fitter and more energetic this season, with Christa Miller also getting more screen time as Dr. Cox’s partner, Jordan. We have yet to see the return of other legacy characters, notably The Janitor (Neil Flynn) and Elliott’s ex-boyfriend Sean Kelly (Scott Foley), both of whom are teased in the trailers for this season.
Over the first two episodes, we follow as he J.D. (Zach Braff) tries to figure out how to best treat Doctor Cox while also dealing with other issues in his new role as Chief of Medicine, including how to be a mentor. The thematic messaging that Scrubs has always balanced with its quirky sense of humor and fantasy cutaway sequences remains intact, but it has aged alongside the cast themselves. While last season dove into the main trio being decades older and dealing with middle age, this season tones that down a bit but still uses age for jokes throughout. The balance of passing the torch to the next generation of medical professionals is the main theme in these early episodes, but it also addresses contemporary issues Gen Z faces in the workplace. New cast member John Higgins ( Please Don’t Destroy ) makes for a good addition to the younger cohort of characters, while YouTuber Daniel Thrasher seems like he may become a bigger presence in subsequent episodes. The loss of cast members X Mayo as charge nurse, Pippa, and Joel Kim Booster as Dr. Kevin Park is minimal, as Rachel Bilson and Tamara Mowry round out the supporting cast nicely.
Something odd I noticed watching these first two episodes was the not-so-subtle marketing. Television has always been a medium for advertising, and in the era of streaming, networks and producers have to find a way to make a profit for the companies that finance these shows. There are multiple shout-outs to P.F. Chang’s restaurant franchise in these two episodes that I may have overlooked had I not watched them back-to-back. Hearing characters specifically name the Asian bistro chain in different contexts is more subtle than other shows like Chuck’s blatant references to Subway during the spy series’ final seasons, but it still feels a bit on the nose for a show that didn’t feature corporate call-outs during its initial run, at least not as overtly as this. I will have to go back and watch the episodes again to see if I missed any others, but I would venture to guess that the rest of the season may reference orange chicken, egg rolls, or other mainstays at P.F. Chang’s.
Showrunners Tim Hobert and Aseem Batra return alongside scribes Mathew Harawitz and Mark Stegemann for the new season. Zach Braff continues to stretch his directing skills this season, while original series creator Bill Lawrence remains an executive producer only rather than directly involved creatively. This season keeps the formula of the classic Scrubs in check with the network sitcom feel of the series, not coming across as stale as we saw in other revivals like Frasier and Murphy Brown. Maybe it is also a credit to the fact that Braff, Faison, and Chalke not only look close to the way they did twenty years ago but can still pull off the physical and energetic sides of their characters, which will still convincingly dive into the pitfalls of getting older in a profession that requires you at the height of your mental skills.
Scrubs thankfully erases the lackluster final seasons of its original run and completely redeems itself with a relaunch that feels as vibrant as the original series while keeping everything that we loved about the classic medical sitcom. At this pace, Scrubs could hang around for multiple years to come, and the transition can be stretched out over several seasons as long as Zach Braff, Donald Faison, and Sara Chalke are willing to do this show. I say let them. It’s always nice to have the comfort and familiarity of characters that you’ve grown up with come back and not feel dated or dragged out of retirement against their will. Scrubs continues to be one of the funniest shows on television and one of the most original and well-written, to boot. I’m looking forward to seeing the rest of the episodes while I wait for my P.F. Chang’s order to arrive via DoorDash.
Scrubs premieres on September 30th on ABC.

articles.title_zh: UK ends 'one in, one out' migrant returns deal with France
articles.content_orig:
The UK's Home Office said on Wednesday that its year-old deal with France to return migrants crossing the Channel on small boats had ended.
"The government's pilot with France to remove asylum seekers in exchange for an equal number of legal migrants is no longer processing new cases," the Home Office said, confirming the end of the so-called "one in, one out" deal, which was launched in August last year and was due to expire on Thursday.
The scheme, known as Operation Hillmore, was part of efforts by London and Paris to tackle illegal migration across the English Channel.
Under the arrangement, Britain could return to France some migrants who arrived illegally by small boat and were judged to have no right to remain in the UK. In exchange, Britain accepted an equal number of asylum seekers from France considered likely to qualify for protection, with priority given to vulnerable nationalities and people with family or other links to the UK.
The two countries agreed in June to extend the pilot until 1 October. The most recent Home Office figures show that 1,087 people were returned to France between 4 August 2025 and 30 June 2026, while 1,117 were transferred to the UK under the scheme. Over the same period, 27,920 migrants arrived in the UK on small boats, meaning only about 4% of arrivals were sent back.
That was one of the clearest signs of the programme's limited impact, despite government claims that it would deter people-smuggling gangs.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood told MPs on 15 September that it cost the UK taxpayer an average of about £56,000 (€65,500) per migrant to return them.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who succeeded Keir Starmer in July, said that Brexit had made stopping small boats harder because the UK no longer had the same level of cooperation with the EU. He declined to set a date for ending the crossings, but told the BBC he and Mahmood would not stop until they had cracked down on "every element of this criminal, illegal activity".
Burnham has said his government is "changing the whole approach" to small boats, pairing tougher enforcement with safe legal routes for asylum seekers, which he argues would take away the smuggling gangs' main selling point.
France's interior minister Laurent Nuñez told lawmakers in June that France wanted a more European approach to illegal migration . He also argued that France should not have to bear sole responsibility for policing an EU external border, blaming weak controls in countries of first entry and onward movement within the Schengen area.
Migrants trying to reach Britain pay smugglers thousands of euros for places on overcrowded inflatable boats to cross one of the world's busiest shipping lanes. Research has also shown a sharp rise this year in small boats setting off from Belgium, as smuggling networks look for new launch points.
Overall, some 197,000 people have crossed the Channel in small boats since the route emerged as a major migration pathway.

These visualisations from exclusive polling modelling show how the UK parliament could change under different voting systems
New analysis produced exclusively for the Guardian reveals how different voting systems would return significantly different seat totals in the UK parliament, based on recent polling.
While the current first past the post (FPTP) system could leave Labour short of a majority with 250 seats, the modelling shows how proportional systems would be likely to reduce the number of seats given to the leading party – and give the UK a more finely balanced parliament that better represents the votes people cast.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has announced a new national commission on electoral reform aimed at changing the electoral system , a plan supported by more than 100 Labour MPs as well as parties such as the Liberal Democrats, the Greens, the SNP and Plaid Cymru. Electoral reform has enjoyed increased public support in recent years .
The research conducted by More in Common suggests that, under proportional systems such as single transferable vote or regional party list, the UK could end up being governed by a minority government – or a progressive alliance of parties.
Proportional representation (PR) aims to produce a parliament that more closely reflects how people voted, allowing voters to back their preferred party without worrying about tactical voting. It often makes it harder for a single party to win a majority and is more likely to result in coalition governments.
Alongside the current first past the post system, More in Common modelled three different PR systems for the Guardian: regional party list, single transferable vote (STV) and additional member system (AMS).
The More in Common research shows that no single party would achieve a majority according to their projected polling, regardless of which system is used.
The current FPTP system would come the closest, giving Labour 39% of the seats off just 26% of the vote – still short of a majority. The party would most likely need the support of the Lib Dems and the SNP to form a majority government.
The proportional systems would not give Labour such a boost: regional party list is estimated to give the party 26% of seats off 26% of the vote; AMS would give it 26% of the seats off 29% of the vote; and STV would give it 27% of the seats off 28% of the vote.
Under each of these systems, either a progressive coalition of parties – a combination of Labour, the Lib Dems, the Greens, the SNP or Plaid Cymru – or a Reform-Conservative-Restore coalition would be the only paths to forming a government. Even then, several scenarios would lead to a minority government in a finely balanced parliament.
While the leading Labour party would lose the largest proportion of seats under the proportional systems, smaller parties would be the biggest winners.
The Green party would win only three seats under FPTP under current polling, but more than 50 seats in all three PR systems that we’re modelling – 9% of the seats on offer, more closely matching their vote share. Likewise, the far-right Restore Britain party would surge above 30 seats in each of the PR systems, compared with winning just one seat under FPTP.
Charlie Buckley, a senior research associate at More in Common, said: “With [Nigel] Farage’s [Reform UK] party having lost some momentum and Andy Burnham being – for now – a more popular prime minister, it’s Labour who would reap the benefits from our current electoral system.
“Despite only being four points ahead of the Tories, our model shows Labour winning double the number of seats under first past the post, while a proportional system would give us a parliament which better reflects the close three-horse race we now have between Labour, Reform and the Conservatives .”
Burnham said in his conference speech that Labour shouldn’t “open the door” to a “divisive government” that could win power on “less than 30% of the vote”.
The proportional systems were more likely to remove the regional dominance of any one party. In London , Labour is estimated to gain 69% of seats under FPTP. This number would drop dramatically under PR, to 37% in the party list system and 42% under AMS.
Reform and the Greens would be the biggest beneficiaries in the capital: while Reform would win one seat and the Greens nothing under FPTP, they’d collectively win 18 seats – nearly a quarter of London’s seats on offer – under the party list system.
The same disparity can be seen in the east of England, with the poll-leaders there, Reform, gaining 43% of the seats under FPTP but falling to 29% under both the party list and AMS systems.

The most recent polling in Britain, as well as recent elections , show an unprecedented fragmentation of the political system. Labour leads on an average of 26%, with Reform second on 23% and the Conservatives third on 20%. The Greens and the Lib Dems are each polling at 10%.
This is based on an average of the last 10 polls, with Labour enjoying a slim lead in the national polls since the party chose Burnham as its new leader and prime minister.
With three parties clustered closely together in the polls, the FPTP system means small shifts in vote share could produce highly volatile and sometimes counterintuitive seat projections , as marginal changes in local contests are amplified into large swings in parliamentary representation.
In the last general election, Labour won 411 of 650 seats with just 34% of the vote.
A report from the Electoral Reform Society modelled the 2024 vote under different voting systems. Only first past the post gave Labour a majority, with all proportional systems giving smaller parties more representation and leading to a hung parliament.
There have been renewed calls for proportional representation. In his conference speech, Burnham said: “We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so that everyone’s vote counts and everyone’s voice is heard.”
Farage has also previously called for electoral reform , calling the current system “outdated” and “not fit for purpose”, but has gone quiet on the subject since Reform went on to lead the polls – until Burnham’s Labour retook a slim lead.
Experts say any attempt to introduce proportional representation for Westminster elections would be likely to face strong pressure for a referendum, given its significance as a constitutional change and the precedent set by the 2011 referendum on the alternative vote system (AV) .
The referendum saw voters decisively reject AV, showing the difficulty of winning public support for electoral reform. Experts warn that any future move to proportional representation could face similar challenges, as voters are familiar with first past the post and may be reluctant to replace a system they already understand.
Buckley said: “The real winners with a PR system would be on the edges of the political spectrum. The Greens would go from a handful of MPs to a sizeable bloc, while Restore Britain would arrive in parliament in numbers, potentially giving these smaller parties a kingmaker role in the formation of coalitions.
“So the prospect of forming a workable majority – already a dubious one in our current electoral system – looks even more complicated under a proportional one. Regardless of the system in place, our fragmented politics would make any election in Britain a challenge for those seeking to enter and control government, and the idea of a ‘commanding majority’ is out of reach for all the major parties right now.”

Sophia Bush and Ashlyn Harris secretly wed one year ago, the actress has revealed in her bombshell new memoir.
One Tree Hill star Bush, 44, and soccer star Harris, 40, tied the knot in a private ceremony in upstate New York in the summer of 2025, and reveal details of the intimate nuptials in Bush's tome, And I Will Tell You Mine: Notes from a Life in Progress.
The couple, who first struck up a romance in 2023 before Bush came out as queer the following year, never publicly announced an engagement and kept their wedding firmly under wraps.
However the pair were seen proudly flashing their wedding rings on a red carpet last week.
'When you get to this stage in your life, you begin to unpack what’s yours and what’s always sort of been for everyone else,' Bush told Vogue of their decision to keep their marriage a secret.
After informing their loved ones of their union, Bush said she was ready to share the marriage with fans, as she did not like calling Harris her 'partner.;'
'You’re not my partner, you know? You’re my wife,' Bush told Harris. 'And it feels so amazing to say that.'
The Daily Mail has contacted representatives for the couple for further comment.

Speaking about their intimate ceremony, which saw the family roast marshmallows after the vows, Harris said, 'The kids were just running and happy, and we picked flowers from the property and our daughter Sloane was holding them. It was so fun for them, because it wasn’t this pressure-filled day that’s too much for young kids.
'It was so precious, and zero pressure. I will never forget it, and I think wedding days sometimes aren’t like that.'

'This conversation is not about Sophia and I. We know the love we share. We understand how sacred and how pure our love is' Harris said.

An excerpt from the memoir obtained by Vogue revealed Bush and Harris both proposed to one another 'a thousand times' before wedding at City Hall in a ceremony officiated by her friend Nia.
Bush wore a black velvet dress with gold flecks while Harris opted for a tuxedo.
After exchanging handwritten vows,  Bush writes, 'We wept. We laughed. We exchanged rings. The invisible string pulled tighter around us.'
This is the second marriage for Harris and third for Bush.
Ali Krieger and Harris exchanged vows in 2019 and adopted their two children together, before announcing their separation in September 2023 and finalizing their divorce in 2025.
Meanwhile, in August 2023, Bush filed for divorce from her second husband Grant Hughes after a marriage that had lasted merely 13 months.
Bush was wed to her One Tree Hill co-star Chad Michael Murray from 2005-2006.
Bush has said she and Harris first became acquainted in 2019 but did not become a couple until October 2023 - after their respective marriages fell apart.
Nevertheless, when romance rumors started swirling about her and Harris, Bush found herself being accused of being a 'home-wrecker.'
Bush firmly denied she broke up Harris' marriage, writing that she had landed on the business end of 'blatant lies and violent threats,' via Glamour .
'People looking in from the outside weren't privy to just how much time it took, how many painful conversations were had,' she insisted.
'A lot of effort was made to be graceful with other people's processing, their time and obligations, and their feelings,' added the Chicago PD actress.
Meanwhile, Harris recently shared her method of weathering the publicity storm that raged around the start of her romance with Bush.
'When all of this news was going crazy, it was really important for me to be intentional that I was a good human during a really hard season that became very public,' said Harris, who played for America at the FIFA Women's World Cup in 2015 and 2019.
'I never wanted to speak ill about the mother of my children in front of them, with other friends. It was really important to me,' she noted.

articles.title_orig: MI5 warns UK academics to cut ties with Chinese group over alleged spying
articles.title_zh: MI5 warns UK academics to cut ties with Chinese group over alleged spying
articles.content_orig:
Britain’s domestic intelligence agency has told academics to stop working with a Chinese organisation funding research in United Kingdom universities, accusing it of having “very strong ties” with China’s spy agency.
In a rare public espionage alert on Wednesday, MI5 alleged the ⁠⁠”primary purpose” of the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) is to finance academic work that improves the espionage capability of the Ministry of State Security (MSS), the Chinese intelligence agency.
There was no immediate response from Beijing, which has previously strongly denied such accusations.
MI5 said the CGTRI targeted more than 100 UK-based academics working in areas such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, covert communications systems and steganography.
It said many academics and institutions would have engaged in good faith with the organisation, unaware of its close ties to the MSS. But it added those who continued to take grants from or work with the CGTRI now risked prosecution under the UK’s National Security Act, a law passed in 2023 that gave the government greater powers to target foreign espionage and hostile state activities.
“This activity supports MSS espionage, which poses a threat to UK national security,” MI5 said.
UK Security Minister ⁠⁠Dan Jarvis said he had written to all university leaders in Britain to ensure staff ended any relationship with the CGTRI.
“This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security, and that of our allies,” he said in a statement.
“International ⁠⁠partnerships are vital to ensure our universities and research institutes continue to thrive, but we will take robust action to defend against the threats we face.”
The UK’s relationship with China, its third largest trading partner, has become ⁠⁠increasingly complex in recent years.
The government in London has sought ⁠⁠better relations with Beijing to improve trade ties and earlier this year approved plans for China to build its largest embassy in Europe in the UK capital. But it has also repeatedly warned of Chinese spying efforts and attempts to undermine the UK’s democratic system.
Last year, Ken McCallum, MI5’s director-general, said Chinese spies were creating fake job adverts to try to dupe British professionals into handing over data.
His agency also issued an alert to UK lawmakers last November that Chinese agents were targeting them to collect information and influence their activity by posing as headhunters or companies.
In ‌‌June, ‌‌security agencies from the Five Eyes intelligence alliance – the US, Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand – published a warning about Chinese spies aggressively using online job platforms to recruit people with access to sensitive information.
China’s London embassy said the warning was “entirely fabricated and constitutes malicious slander”.

articles.title_orig: Court Pauses Execution of Tennessee’s Lone Woman on Death Row
articles.title_zh: Court Pauses Execution of Tennessee’s Lone Woman on Death Row
articles.content_orig:
A federal appeals court has temporarily stopped Tennessee from executing death row inmate Christa Pike , intervening less than two hours before she was due to receive a lethal injection.
The 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals granted what it called a “short stay of execution” on Wednesday while judges consider Pike’s argument that evidence of sexual abuse she experienced as a child was not properly weighed when she was sentenced.
Tennessee officials quickly turned to the US Supreme Court, asking the justices to lift the stay and allow the execution to proceed.
Pike, 50, had been scheduled to die at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Had the execution gone ahead, she would have been the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than two centuries.
She was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate at a Knoxville vocational centre.
Pike was 18 when she, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, and another teenager tortured and killed Slemmer. Pike and Shipp were later convicted of first-degree murder. Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Pike’s lawyers have argued that her childhood was marked by violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including rapes when she was 11 and 17 years old. They also cited her later diagnoses of bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder in seeking to have her sentence reduced to life without parole.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee rejected that clemency request. Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has publicly supported the execution.
The case has also attracted international scrutiny, with a group of United Nations human rights experts calling for Pike’s death sentence to be commuted.
Women have accounted for just 18 of the 1,683 executions carried out in the US since capital punishment resumed in 1976. Pike’s case is more unusual still: If the execution ultimately proceeds, she would be the only person in Tennessee’s modern death penalty era put to death for a crime committed as a teenager.

articles.title_orig: Senate Democrats block bill to limit lawmakers' stock trades, citing voter ID provision
articles.title_zh: Senate Democrats block bill to limit lawmakers' stock trades, citing voter ID provision
articles.content_orig:
Washington — A Republican-led effort to approve a House-passed stock trading bill fell short in the Senate on Wednesday, with Democrats arguing the restrictions don't go far enough while pushing back against a voter ID provision that they argue would gut mail voting.
In a 53 to 47 vote that fell along party lines, the measure failed to reach a 60-vote threshold needed to advance.
The bill, known as the Stop Insider Trading Act, passed the House in July with the support of all Republicans and 13 Democrats. It would prohibit lawmakers, their spouses and dependent children, from purchasing publicly traded stocks, while requiring that they publicly disclose each intended sale at least a week in advance to limit their ability to profit off insider information.
But Democrats argued that the bill doesn't go far enough, urging that an outright ban is needed for members of Congress — along with the president and members of his administration.
"The Republican toothless stock-trading bill is as ineffective as a screen door on a submarine," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said on the Senate floor ahead of the vote. "And let's be clear: they don't even want it to pass. They designed the bill to fail."
The New York Democrat railed against the legislation earlier this week, while noting it wouldn't apply to the executive branch. He claimed that Republicans "carved the White House out of their supposed crack down on corruption."
Democrats also saw the bill's provision requiring voters to show photo identification when voting in federal elections as a poison pill designed to prompt them to vote against the more popular stock-trading restrictions. The unrelated provision was included in the bill as President Trump has put pressure on Congress to approve elections-related legislation ahead of the midterms.
GOP leaders moved ahead with the vote on Wednesday as senators prepare to leave town to hit the campaign trail, bringing up the vote alongside another bill aimed at shielding Americans from energy costs attributed to data centers later in the day. The votes, which were expected to fall short, aimed to put Democrats on the record on the issues at a time when Senate Republicans face several races that have grown more competitive, putting control of the upper chamber next year into question.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, called the bill a "common-sense piece of legislation," pointing to its limits on stock trading and the voter ID requirement.
"It's a pretty simple measure," Thune said. "But an important way to ensure that members of Congress are held to the standards that America should be able to expect of their representatives."
Lawmakers have pursued a number of efforts to ban congressional stock trading in recent years. But Schumer argued that the latest bill "isn't a stock-trading ban, it's Republicans' last-ditch effort to save face." If Republicans want to ban stock trading, the New York Democrat said his caucus is "ready to go."

articles.title_zh: ‘We don’t need boos’: Astros players frustrated as own fans turn on them in playoffs
articles.content_orig:
On morning service from Dubai to Tel Aviv, 150 passengers witnessed a horrific cockpit assault and a daring rescue
Pilot who stabbed co-pilot on Israel-bound plane may have tried to crash it, says Netanyahu
A s flight FZ 1073 soared west over the waters of the Gulf towards Israel , its passengers may have bemoaned a 20-minute delay at takeoff. For a low-cost airline route, flydubai’s daily service to Tel Aviv is usually convenient and reliable. The nonstop flight takes about three and a half hours and departs early enough from Dubai that it usually lands at Ben Gurion airport at about 9am local time.
That was not the case for Wednesday’s catastrophic flight. The passenger jet never made it to its scheduled destination. Instead, it dropped thousands of feet in seconds before limping down to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia – perhaps miraculously, since photos suggested a large part of the tail of the aircraft was missing.
Passengers evacuated, some covered in blood, with stories to share of a pilot-on-pilot stabbing, and footage posted online from inside the fuselage showed the aftermath of violence.
In one video, two men lie on the floor with breathing masks on their faces as passengers stand over them in the cramped gangway. One wears a white shirt soaked red with blood, and the distinctive pilot stripes on his shoulders. He appears almost unresponsive. The other man blinks slowly, with blood smeared on the wall next to him. A person off camera appears to encourage the injured man to remain conscious: “No sleep,” he says.
More footage, apparently from a seat further back, shows passengers screaming and weeping in distress as the Boeing 737 Max shakes. Israeli media reported that the plane was carrying about 150 Israeli passengers.
Accounts from the airline, passenger testimony, flight trackers and Israeli officials describe a series of horrific events starting about two and a half hours after takeoff.
The flight tracking website Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft abruptly descending from its cruising altitude of about 34,000ft to 17,000ft in less than two minutes. Investigators will look at whether such a sudden and ferocious movement was the reason for damage to the aircraft’s rudder.
Minutes later, the plane sent out a series of emergency transponder signals in the form of “squawk codes”. These four-digit codes are normally used by pilots to broadcast their position but can be used in an emergency situation, even if pilots are in radio contact with air traffic control.
Aircraft trackers at Flightradar24 said the flydubai plane transmitted emergency and hijack signals. The aircraft made an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border before turning around and heading south.
In one video, a passenger with blood dripping from an open wound on his head pleads for assistance and says the jet is descending into Saudi Arabia. “Whoever is hearing me, we need help,” the man says in Hebrew. “We are in the Tabuk area of Saudi Arabia, which we don’t know. All the passengers are OK except for the pilot. We need help.”
What was happening during these critical minutes is still being investigated, but early unconfirmed reports pointed to a cockpit fight, followed by passengers storming up the aisle, and then either one or more pilots who were travelling as passengers wresting control of the plane to avert a disaster.
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz cited a passenger as saying that the plane lost control and began to dive.
Dalia Shpigel was quoted as saying that “suddenly there were terrible screams throughout the plane” before “three to five guys burst into the cockpit” and subdued the alleged assailant and began treating an injured pilot.
“We realised that the situation was stabilising and continued the flight. Gradually, information began to emerge about what had happened in the cockpit,” Shpigel told Haaretz.
Her fellow passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the “co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane”.
Speaking to reporters via speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion airport, she said the plane “was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him”.
“There was also a doctor who gave first aid, and people who treated both of them … but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do,” she said.
The Emirati carrier, in a statement later on Wednesday, said the aircraft was “successfully secured by on-duty flydubai crew travelling on the flight”, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport. Airlines often move pilots around different airports as passengers, and it is possible it was these pilots who sent the emergency codes.
One passenger, Almog Itali, was quoted by the BBC as saying that one of the pilots onboard who stabilised the plane was British. “There were two spare pilots who were supposed to operate the next flight,” he said. “The relief pilots are European, one of them British, who entered [the cockpit] and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia.”
Stanislav Bukhman, the head of risk at Osprey Flight Solutions, an aviation security firm based in the UK, said investigators were likely to focus on a few key areas, including how pilots were vetted, and crew screening at the departure airport.
On how the flight deck might have been accessed, he said cabin crew could request entry to the cockpit using an emergency access code. “This exists for situations where the pilots are incapacitated. There is a safeguard built in, though. If the pilots are conscious and operating normally, they can deny that request and keep the door locked. This is designed to protect the flight deck in a hijacking or hostage situation,” he said.
“At this stage there isn’t enough information to say how the flight deck on FZ 1073 was accessed. The door may have been opened by the captain, who reportedly resisted the co-pilot’s attempt to take control, or by cabin crew using the emergency procedure.”
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, announced that one of the pilots had planned to crash and kill its mostly Israeli passengers, who stopped a “major disaster” with their actions. The alleged assailant was arrested after the plane landed, Netanyahu ‌said.
“During the flight, as they approached the country, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone onboard,” Netanyahu said in a video message, calling the passengers “heroes”. All the passengers were accounted for and safe.
Flydubai, however, said an “altercation” occurred in the flight deck of flight FZ 1073, and it warned against drawing conclusions about the motive.
“At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation,” a flydubai spokesperson said in a statement. “We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

American troops are scheduled to exit their final military posts in Iraq on Wednesday, a pullout welcomed as a triumph by Iran and its partners. Their sway runs deep across the country, where over two decades of fighting claimed 4,500 U.S. lives.
Nevertheless, the United States has retained practical power over Iraq's oil revenue since its 2003 invasion. That financial leverage grants Washington immense control over affairs in Baghdad, carrying significant implications for regional dynamics involving Iran.
At the center of the issue is how the Federal Reserve Bank of New York handles Iraq's oil earnings.
Following the 2003 military campaign, the American-led Coalition Provisional Authority (CPA) created the Development Fund for Iraq (DFI). Housed at the New York Fed, this mechanism was established to gather energy income intended for national rebuilding and redevelopment projects.
The initiative was also structured to safeguard these assets from legal actions and claims originating from Saddam Hussein's regime.
Formed under an executive directive from then-President George W. Bush, the system has been extended by every president since. The DFI was ultimately converted into a Central Bank of Iraq account at the New York Federal Reserve, where it continues to operate.
Generating roughly 90 percent of its total state budget, crude oil is Iraq's primary economic resource, giving Washington considerable influence over the nation's political and financial stability.
When Iraqi leaders requested the withdrawal of American forces in 2020, Washington reportedly threatened to block access to Baghdad's New York Federal Reserve accounts, forcing the government to back down.
Although Iraq has gained greater authority over its financial matters since the initial occupation years, this connection underscores the US's lasting influence on the Iraqi economy, even as the country tries to assert full political independence and national sovereignty.
Iraq's financial stability has been secured by the mechanism, which protects public funds, government sources told Reuters anonymously.
According to officials, the framework strengthens international trust in oil revenue oversight, facilitates access to American currency required for commercial trade and imports, and shields state income from external legal claims, creditor demands, and broader economic shocks.
The setup stabilizes exchange rates and reinforces faith in the national economy, helping fortify local financial institutions while asserting broader economic control, officials added.
It also gives the government leverage to push back against factions, including Iran-backed groups, that demand fewer restrictions on dollar access. Last year, the U.S. targeted several Iraqi banks and figures with sanctions over allegations of money laundering for Tehran.
Heavy curbs on U.S. dollar supply led to a parallel, informal market for dollars, creating a price spread between the central bank's official exchange rate and the black-market rate. The ​price difference is essentially a risk premium for dealing outside the formal system. In his second term,
​Trump has pursued a ⁠campaign of maximum pressure on Iran , with Iraq often caught in the crossfire as Tehran has used it as a vital economic lung. The war he launched with Israel against Iran on February 28 added further pressure on Baghdad.
The Federal Reserve Bank of New York continues to hold custody of Iraq's oil earnings.
To supply American dollars, the CBI traditionally relied on dollar auctions, officially known as the foreign currency window. This allowed private banks and exchange firms to bid daily for U.S. currency using Iraqi dinars.
Under heavy U.S. pressure, Iraq officially shuttered this auction framework in early 2025, driven by a broader crackdown targeting the alleged siphoning of dollars to sanctioned parties, particularly Iran.

articles.title_orig: Romania’s political crisis intensifies as Parliament rejects pro-EU PM
articles.title_zh: Romania’s political crisis intensifies as Parliament rejects pro-EU PM
articles.content_orig:
Romania’s pro-European Prime Minister-designate Siegfried Muresan has failed to win a parliamentary vote of confidence, prolonging a political crisis seen as a boost for the rising far right.
Muresan, a liberal European Parliament member who was the latest of three designated prime ministers, secured only 182 votes out of the 233 required to secure the confidence motion on Wednesday, according to the official count.
The far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) largely boycotted the vote.
The 45-year-old had proposed what he described as a “reform-oriented” governing programme under his centre-right National Liberal Party (PNL), which teamed up with the Save Romania Union party, or USR, and the small ethnic Hungarian UDMR party.
President Nicusor Dan said he would nominate a new prime minister candidate on Monday afternoon, after holding talks with the leaders of the parliamentary parties, to avoid snap elections.
Romania saw the collapse of a pro-European coalition government in May, when governing social democrats, together with the opposition far right, ousted liberal Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan in a no-confidence motion at that time.
The far right, which comprises about a third of Parliament, threatened to impeach the president if he does not call early elections once the conditions are met.
Romania, a member of the EU and NATO that borders Ukraine, has not held snap elections since the fall of communism in 1989.
Political analyst Cristian Pirvulescu told the AFP news agency that snap elections would lead to another fragmented Parliament, but with an emboldened far right.
“Early elections mean that, from the moment they are called, it would take four months before a new government could be formed,” Pirvulescu told AFP. “Due to political instability, Romania finds itself in a very complicated economic situation. Four months is already a very long time.”
The country of 19 million has been struggling for months with the highest public deficit and inflation in the European Union.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is taking a ‘long-term view’ of Microsoft’s gaming division.
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has denied reports that Microsoft is considering selling off its Xbox business. The Information reported in June that Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and CFO Amy Hood had been considering spinning out Xbox entirely, and then reported earlier this month that both execs have “more recently supported Sharma’s plans to overhaul the unit.”
“Xbox is not for sale,” says Sharma in an interview with The New York Times . “We will do whatever it takes to set the company up for success, and we will look at the right partnerships, the right operating model and everything needed to achieve that.”
It appears that Nadella and Hood have favored the giant Xbox “reset” as the plan for Microsoft’s gaming unit instead of making Xbox a joint venture or spinning out the gaming business entirely. Sharma announced her Xbox restructuring in June, calling it a reset for the division. Microsoft is planning to lay off up to 3,200 Xbox employees over the course of its 2027 financial year, which ends in June.
Nadella backed Sharma’s restructuring and layoffs in a recent appearance on the Sources podcast . “There’s some amount of streamlining the team is doing, and Asha is doing, which is great to see,” said Nadella last week. “And then we have to invent the right sustainable business model that allows us to deliver gaming to more and more people.”
The most recent restructuring has seen Halo move under Activision, as well as the developers behind Sea of Thieves and Age of Empires . Alongside a major shake-up of Xbox Game Studios, the recent changes look geared toward making Xbox a wholly owned subsidiary like Microsoft does with LinkedIn.
Microsoft is reducing management layers at Xbox, offloading smaller studios, and focusing on its larger Xbox franchises. That could eventually end in an Xbox sale at some point in the future, but right now the plan seems to be about bringing growth back to Xbox. “We’ve got a long way to go with Microsoft,” says Sharma, “and we’re going to take the long-term view.”
But as Sharma said in February , “The plan’s the plan until it’s not the plan.”

articles.title_orig: Scrubs Returns for Season 11, and the Beloved Medical Sitcom Is Funnier and More Heartwarming Than Ever
articles.title_zh: Scrubs Returns for Season 11, and the Beloved Medical Sitcom Is Funnier and More Heartwarming Than Ever
articles.content_orig:
The first two episodes of Scrubs Season 11 premiere on ABC on September 30 and on Hulu on October 1.
In an era where it's become customary to wait years between new seasons of many popular shows, it's certainly a treat to receive two seasons of Scrubs in the same calendar year. The previous revival season proved to be the ultimate sitcom comfort food. It effortlessly wiped away the stigma of Season 9 and won fans back over with its depiction of the eternal bromance between Drs. John Dorian (Zach Braff) and Christopher Turk (Donald Faison). Season 10 wasn't without its problems, but it was a fun little romp that recaptured the charming vibe of the original series. Season 11 is much the same, but with a slightly more ambitious storytelling approach added for good measure.
Naturally, Braff and Faison remain in the spotlight for Season 11, as does Sarah Chalke's Dr. Elliot Reid. Much of the new cast introduced in Season 10 also returns, with Ava Bunn's Sam Tosh now upped to series regular. Unfortunately, Season 11 eliminates two of the more memorable supporting cast members in Joel Kim Booster's Dr. Kevin Park and X Mayo's Nurse Pippa Raymond. It's not the worst thing in the world for the series to trim its ensemble cast a bit, but neither character deserved to be on the chopping block.
Season 10 did suffer at times from the lack of focus on classic Scrubs characters like Dr. Cox (John C. McGinley) and Nurse Carla Espinosa (Judy Reyes). Thankfully, that changed late in the game as the now-retired Dr. Cox came roaring back into Sacred Heart and grappled with his own mortality. One of the perks of Season 11 is that it continues that storyline rather than simply moving on. In fact, there are hints of a more serialized narrative this season. The show really leans into Cox's ongoing health struggles and J.D.'s desperate attempts to care for his prickly mentor. Mind you, Scrubs is in no danger of turning into The Pitt anytime soon, but it is nice to get a bit more drama and see a little more connective tissue between these first two episodes. And if that approach keeps McGinley's hilarious character in the picture longer this season, so much the better.
If Scrubs is being a bit more ambitious with its storytelling this season, it certainly never loses sight of the fact that fans are here first and foremost for the dynamic between J.D., Turk, and Elliot. All three characters get ample room to shine in these first two episodes. J.D and Turk have several memorable bonding scenes together, and the series is ever on-point with J.D.'s fanciful dream sequences. There's one cutaway that rivals Season 10's detective noir scene for its sheer zaniness. And with Elliot, the series continues finding ways to explore and enrich the character outside the shackles of the "Will they, won't they?" format the original series was so fixated on.
But what of the newbies? As enjoyable as it was, Season 10 never fully cemented its new cast of interns. There were simply too many of these characters, and they never felt like a priority for the series amid the emphasis on the core doctor trinity. These two episodes show signs that the writers are looking to narrow their focus a bit this time. Obviously, Bunn's Tosh is a bigger priority now, and Episode 2 makes some inroads in terms of defining her as more than "the social media-obsessed one."
In fact, Episode 2, which is titled "My Mentee," seems to cement a new status quo where each of the three leads is paired with a different underling, mirroring the Cox/J.D. dynamic of the original show. Elliott gets Tosh, Turk gets Dr. Dashana Trainor (Amanda Morrow), and J.D. struggles to connect with the new chief resident, Dr. Grant Summers (John Higgins). This narrowed focus is promising, though it does serve to make the rest of the interns like Asher (Jacob Dudman) and Blake (David Gridley) feel even more superfluous than before. We'll see if Season 11 can ultimately achieve a better balance than its predecessor, but things are looking promising so far.
Scrubs Season 11 loses none of the momentum of Season 10 in its first two episodes. The series is as effortlessly charming and silly as ever. The show even looks to improve on its predecessor in some key ways. There's a hint of a darker, more serialized narrative this time around, and there's a concerted effort to rein in the unruly cast of supporting characters too. Fans of the series will find plenty to love with this new season.

The Trump administration said it will start sending refund checks on Wednesday to Affordable Care Act enrollees across the U.S. who it says were "overcharged" by the Biden administration.
Nearly 1 million Americans across 30 states will receive the $500 checks, along with a letter from President Trump.
"For years, the Biden Administration overcharged you to fund the operation of HealthCare.gov," Mr. Trump says in the letter, a copy of which was shared with CBS News. "That money belongs to hard-working Americans, not the Government, and now, I am returning it to you!"
Some families with more than one "affected person" could receive multiple payments via check or direct deposit, an administration official told CBS News. The primary recipients of the checks will be people who earn above 400% of the federal poverty line, the official added.
The states where people are getting refunds rely on federal exchanges administered by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which charges a user fee. The White House said earlier this month that it is issuing the refunds because the Biden administration overcharged Americans through those fees and then passed it on to consumers in the form of higher premium costs — what it referred to as a "gross mismanagement of Obamacare."
"With this Historic Action, my Administration is taking the surplus funds that accumulated from the ObamacarePremium Taxand issuing a one-time $500 REFUND to Americans who use the HealthCare.gov platform to purchase their health insurance, but who do not receive Taxpayer Subsidies to pay for their Coverage," the president said in his letter.
Millions of Obamacare recipients are facing higher premiums after Congress last year allowed coverage subsidies to expire. In a KFF poll released in March, half of the respondents said their premiums, deductibles or other costs are "a lot higher" than they were last year.
The Trump administration's refund effort comes with just over a month to go until the midterm elections and as affordability concerns are weighing on many households. High inflation and gas prices due to the war with Iran have pushed the president's approval ratings on the economy to near-record lows.

articles.title_orig: DOJ ramps up fight against federal judges after some in Minnesota speak to media about immigration surge cases
articles.title_zh: DOJ ramps up fight against federal judges after some in Minnesota speak to media about immigration surge cases
articles.content_orig:
Washington — The Justice Department took the unusual step on Wednesday of filing a judicial misconduct complaint against all but one of the federal district judges in Minnesota, after most of them spoke with the New York Times about concerns over the government's handling of cases during its surge in immigration enforcement earlier this year.
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the filing of the complaint with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit at a press conference, where he also said that prosecutors in Minnesota had secured an indictment against 10 noncitizens for allegedly casting votes unlawfully in prior elections.
"We have a right, just like every litigant in court, to have a judge that will be fair and impartial," Blanche said. "We have no choice but to act."
At the heart of the complaint is a New York Times story published earlier this month headlined "Trump's Minnesota Surge Threatened Democracy, Judge Warns." As a part of the story, Judge Patrick Schiltz sat for a 90-minute interview and shared his views on what he said were repeated violations of court orders by the Trump administration. The article said that six of the seven members of Minnesota's federal bench also spoke with reporters to discuss the federal government's immigration crackdown in the state, called Operation Metro Surge.
Schiltz was appointed to the federal bench by President George W. Bush and clerked for Justice Antonin Scalia on the Supreme Court.
The judicial misconduct complaint names Schiltz and Judge John Tunheim, appointed by President Bill Clinton, as well as "anonymous district judges" serving on the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota. In the article, Tunheim pushed back on the Trump administration's claim that it was arresting the "worst of the worst" in Minnesota.
"They weren't arresting, in my view, people who were dangerous criminals on the street," Tunheim told the Times.
The Justice Department said Schiltz and Tunheim's conduct "is particularly egregious" and claimed the two "flagrantly violated the Code of Judicial Conduct with their improper and unethical comments" to the Times.
The complaint is signed by Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter and Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward.
The officials said Schiltz's comments in particular were "overly political and concern matters that are pending," either before the judge or an appeals court. They said that Tunheim's comment was "less verbose" but "equally unethical."
"If anything is a 'grave threat to the rule of law,' it is judges who repeatedly and brazenly exceed their authority then launch a partisan press campaign that includes criticizing the government for filing an emergency appeal when a judge refused to rule on a search warrant application," McCotter and Woodward wrote.
They asked the 8th Circuit to order Schiltz and Tunheim to recuse themselves from matters involving the Department of Homeland Security. They said the appeals court should also launch an investigation into the "improper conduct" of Minnesota judges who "'covet publicity' rather than adhering to the rule of law by adjudicating cases or controversies."
The Trump administration launched Operation Metro Surge in December 2025 and deployed more than 3,000 immigration authorities to Minnesota as part of its immigration enforcement campaign. Border czar Tom Homan announced in February that Operation Metro Surge would be coming to an end and there would be a drawdown of federal immigration officers in the state.
But the stepped-up immigration actions led to violent clashes between federal authorities and protesters. Two people, Renee Good and Alex Pretti , were killed in Minnesota in January, sparking criticism of the tactics used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection.
In the federal courts, judges in Minnesota were inundated with scores of petitions from migrants challenging their detentions and asking to be freed. In a pair of extraordinary orders issued in the case of an Ecuadorian man, Schiltz accused the Trump administration of failing to respond to "dozens" of court orders. He identified 96 court orders in 74 cases that he said ICE had violated.
"ICE is not a law unto itself," he wrote in one order issued Jan. 28.
In another, from two days earlier, Schiltz said the Trump administration "decided to send thousands of agents to Minnesota to detain aliens without making any provision for dealing with the hundreds of habeas petitions and other lawsuits that were sure to result" and said "the court's patience is at an end."

Eventually Trump himself released the document as a âWhite House Accord on Super Intelligence,â outlining broad principles for self-regulation.

It also suggests that his political clout can rival that of the free-spending Musk and Huang â who recently made headlines by speaking to the president onstage at an industry conference.

The accord, signed by Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google, and NVIDIA, lays out a commitment to ârobust internal controlsâ and outside audits designed to ensure the safety of frontier AI models. Some of those models abide by a voluntary clearance by the government under a framework established by a Trump order on AI, though that framework was never released to the public.

Carnegie Mellon University just received a historic $3 billion donation from Citadel CEO Ken Griffin.
Carnegie Mellon, which is located in Pittsburgh , announced the gift Wednesday morning. The university says it intends to use $2 billion to open a new campus in Miami , called Carnegie Mellon University Miami.
“We are deeply grateful to Ken Griffin for his extraordinary vision, partnership and belief in what Carnegie Mellon can achieve,” CMU President Farnam Jahanian said in a statement.
Construction is scheduled to begin in 2027 and should be open to new students in 2028, presuming there are no major regulatory hurdles, according to the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette .
Griffin bought the 35 acres in Wynwood, Florida, where the university will be built, for $1.1 billion from real estate developer Moishe Mana.
Mana said that the sale is the largest land assemblage deal in Florida history.
The campus is expected to support more than 3,500 undergraduate, master's and PhD students, plus approximately 300 faculty members and more than 600 staff.
The university said in a statement that the new school will focus its education on confronting “societal challenges” rather than on traditional academic majors.
The statement said it will focus on “challenge areas spanning human health and biological discovery; national security and strategic capabilities; energy and climate resilience; and advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation.”
The university reportedly had to “rethink” how it operates to respond to the rise of AI.
“Artificial intelligence represents one of the defining intellectual developments of our time, and it demands that we rethink how we educate students, conduct research and partner with others,” Jahanian said.
The final $1 billion of the donation will go to support Carnegie Mellon's Pittsburgh campus. Approximately half will be used to boost the university's highest priority needs, and another half will be invested in its School of Computer Science, which will be renamed the Kenneth C. Griffin School of Computer Science in his honor.
CMU said that the donation is the largest individual donor gift ever given to a university. Before Griffin’s gift, the largest individual donation to a university was Michael Bloomberg’s $1.8 billion donation to Johns Hopkins University in 2018.
This isn’t Griffin’s first investment in South Florida. He attended high school in the region, and moved Citadel’s headquarters from Chicago to Miami in 2022. He explained the move at the time by insisting that Florida had a better corporate environment than Illinois.
He said earlier this year he planned to give fewer resources to Citadel’s presence in New York and more to its efforts in South Florida. He made that decision following a public spat with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani over a wealth tax in April.
While discussing his proposed tax in April, Mamdani called out Griffin directly, noting that he maintained a $238 million penthouse in the city while others were struggling to find homes due to a lack of affordable housing.
“We went to Miami and revised our building plan to make it a bigger office building,” Griffin said in May. “What the mayor of New York has made clear to my partners, and principally my New York partners, is that we need to double down on our bet in Miami.”

articles.title_orig: GOP senator urges ICE to dial back enforcement sweeps
articles.title_zh: GOP senator urges ICE to dial back enforcement sweeps
articles.content_orig:
Republican senator Jim Justice of West Virginia criticizes immigration crackdown as ranchers’ associations condemn ICE activity
A close political ally of Donald Trump has broken from the administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement agenda and recommended it “step back” to evaluate what it could do better.
“To get better, the first thing you got to do is admit you’re doing something wrong,” Jim Justice, a Republican senator of West Virginia, told Politico . “And in this situation, with all that’s going on and all the stuff, we probably got to step back from it and say: ‘Maybe we’re doing something wrong here or there,’ and then adjust to that.”
Justice, who also sits on the Senate agriculture committee, made his comments after three rancher associations condemned Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity for negatively affecting agricultural communities.
But his comments also come after an ACLU of West Virginia investigation found that about three-quarters of the more than 593 arrested by ICE in the state during “Operation Country Roads” in January had no criminal record.
“Before you know it, you get people that get carried away in their job and whatever it may be, and all of a sudden, then you’re dragging people away that have lived on your street corner for 15 years, and I don’t know that we need to be doing that stuff,” Justice told Politico.
Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda is a signature policy of his administration. Many voters indicated they wanted stricter immigration policies, but the intense tactics of federal agents have sparked anger nationwide.
For ranchers in rural communities, ICE operations have had “a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers” who assist in beef production and the cattle supply chain, the Kansas Livestock Association, Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association and Texas Cattle Feeders Association said in a statement released last week.
Dairy farmers have also recently raised concerns that ICE operations in rural areas could soon hurt their industries.
“If we had a concerted effort to have enforcement activities within agriculture, you could really harm our ability to produce food to feed ourselves,” Rick Naerebout, the CEO of the Idaho Dairymen’s Association, told NPR .
West Virginia is home to more than 22,700 ranchers , most of which are family-owned.
Justice’s criticisms make him the latest Republican to distance himself from Trump in the lead-up to the midterm elections.
Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican congresswoman from Florida, recently ran a campaign advertisement telling Trump his “immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far”.
The Guardian has asked the White House for a response.
